title: Postgres backup and restore runbook
text: Postgres backup and restore runbook for the orders cluster. This runbook covers the nightly backup job, WAL archiving, and the restore procedure we actually drill. Read the whole thing before touching production; the restore section has ordering constraints that are easy to get wrong. Our durability story has two layers, base backups and continuous WAL archiving, and both have to be healthy for point-in-time recovery to work. Base backups run nightly at 02:30 UTC from the standby replica. We take them with pg_basebackup using checkpoint mode fast, and the job runs against the replica rather than the primary so the checkpoint spike never lands on live traffic. A full base backup of the orders cluster is currently about 180 GB and takes a little under an hour. The backup job writes a manifest with the end-of-backup LSN, and the monitoring check compares that LSN against the primary every morning. WAL segments are archived continuously to the S3 bucket db-wal-archive with a 35 day retention policy. Retention on the base backups matches, so any moment in the last five weeks is recoverable. If WAL archiving falls more than 15 minutes behind, the on-call gets paged, because a gap in the WAL stream makes every later base backup useless for point-in-time recovery. Archive failures are almost always S3 credential rotation gone wrong, so check the credentials first. Restores are the part people get wrong under pressure. Never restore over the existing data directory; always restore into a fresh directory and repoint the service. The procedure is: fetch the latest base backup, unpack it, write a recovery signal file, set restore_command to pull from db-wal-archive, and set the recovery target time. Postgres replays WAL until the target and then pauses, which gives you a chance to inspect before promoting. Only promote once the application owner confirms the data looks right; promotion is a one-way door. We drill this restore quarterly, and the target is a full restore in 45 minutes or less. The last drill came in at 38 minutes end to end. The drill restores into the staging VPC from production backups, which also proves the backups are actually readable and not just present. Common failure modes: restore_command pointing at the wrong bucket path, forgetting the recovery signal file so postgres boots straight into normal mode, and drilling with a recovery target newer than the last archived segment. The runbook owner is the storage team; changes go through review like any other code. If you find a step that does not match reality, fix the runbook in the same PR as the fix. Backup health is reported on the storage dashboard, and the weekly ops review looks at the age of the newest verified restore. A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup.

title: Postmortem: cache stampede in the catalog service
text: Postmortem: cache stampede in the product catalog service. On March 14 the catalog API returned elevated errors and timeouts for 41 minutes, from 09:12 to 09:53 UTC. This document is blameless; the goal is to fix the system, not to find a person. Impact: roughly 8 percent of catalog requests failed or timed out, and checkout conversion dipped while product pages loaded slowly. During the stampede p99 latency peaked at 2.4 seconds against a normal p99 of 180 milliseconds. The catalog service caches rendered product data in Redis in front of the catalog database. Cache entries were written with a fixed TTL, and that uniformity is the whole story of this incident. The root cause was a fixed 90 second TTL that let the entire set of hot keys expire in the same instant. The hot keys had all been populated together by the 09:10 cache warmer run, so ninety seconds later they all vanished together. Every request that missed the cache went to the database, and the database connection pool saturated within seconds. Saturated connections made cache refills slow, which kept the cache empty, which sent more traffic to the database; the loop fed itself. The service retried timed-out database queries once, which added load exactly when the database had none to spare. Recovery began when the warmer repopulated the hot set and the connection pool drained. What went well: the alert on database pool saturation fired within 2 minutes, and the dashboard made the miss-rate spike obvious. What went poorly: nobody connected the warmer schedule to the expiry wave until 25 minutes in, and the runbook for the catalog service had no entry for cache misses as a cause of database overload. Where we got lucky: the incident started before peak traffic; two hours later the same expiry wave would have been significantly worse. The fix that shipped: cache writes now use a jittered TTL of 90 seconds plus a random extension of up to 30 percent, so expiries spread instead of aligning. We also capped concurrent database refills per key with a single-flight lock, so a thousand misses on one key become one database query. Follow-ups, in priority order: move the warmer to staggered batches, add a dashboard panel correlating cache miss rate with database pool usage, and load-test the refill path with the cache flushed. Action items have owners and dates in the tracker; the lock work shipped with the TTL change. The lesson worth keeping: a cache with synchronized expiry is a scheduled outage. Uniform TTLs look tidy and behave like a countdown. Jitter is not an optimization, it is the difference between a cache and a time bomb.

title: Design: rate limiting for the public API
text: Design: rate limiting for the public API. This document proposes per-key rate limits at the edge, the algorithm, the response contract, and the abuse tier. Goals: protect shared backends from a single hot client, keep limits predictable for integrators, and fail in a way clients can program against. Non-goals: fairness between endpoints of one key, and billing enforcement, which stays in the billing service. We evaluated fixed windows, sliding windows, and token buckets. Fixed windows allow a burst of double the limit at the window edge, and sliding window logs cost memory per request; the token bucket gives smooth limits with a controlled burst at constant memory. Each API key gets a token bucket holding 100 requests that refills at 10 requests per second. The bucket size is the burst allowance and the refill rate is the sustained limit; both are per key, not per IP, because NAT makes IP-based limits punish the wrong people. Bucket state lives in the gateway Redis, one hash per key, refilled lazily on access from the elapsed time. Enforcement happens in the API gateway, not in each backend service, so every service is protected the day it launches and limits are configured in exactly one place. The gateway rejects over-limit requests without forwarding them, which is the whole point: a rejected request must cost us almost nothing. When a request is rejected the response is a 429 with a Retry-After header, and the header value is rounded up to whole seconds because fractional seconds tempt clients into tight retry loops. The response body repeats the limit, the remaining tokens, and the reset time in JSON, and successful responses carry the same fields as X-RateLimit headers so clients can pace themselves before hitting the wall. Clients that keep sending while limited are the abuse case. Keys that exceed ten thousand rejected requests in an hour move to the abuse tier automatically. The abuse tier shrinks the bucket to 5 requests refilling at 1 request per 10 seconds, and release from the tier is manual, by support, on purpose. We considered returning 503 for abusive keys and rejected it; 503 tells a well-behaved retry layer to try again, which is exactly the wrong message. Observability: the gateway emits per-key accept and reject counters, and the dashboard tracks the reject ratio by tier. An alert fires if global rejects exceed 5 percent of traffic, because that usually means a limit is misconfigured, not that the internet turned hostile. Rollout: shadow mode first, logging would-be rejections without enforcing, for two weeks. Shadow mode found three internal services that would have been limited immediately; internal traffic now bypasses the public limits through a separate gateway listener. Open questions: whether large integrators get negotiated buckets, and whether the abuse tier needs an appeal path faster than support tickets. Limits are a product surface, not just a defense. Clients build against whatever behavior we ship, so the contract in this document is the part we will never be able to change casually.

title: Deployment guide for the web platform clusters
text: Deployment guide for the web platform clusters. Every service on the platform deploys the same way: a rolling update driven by the deploy pipeline, gated by health checks, reversible in one command. Deploys are boring here by design, and this guide is what keeps them boring. The pipeline builds an image, pins it by digest, and updates the Deployment manifest in the environment repo; the cluster reconciles from git, so kubectl apply by hand is both unnecessary and audited against. Rolling updates run with maxSurge set to 25 percent and maxUnavailable set to 0, so capacity never drops during a deploy and the cluster briefly runs extra pods instead. That surge costs headroom: clusters keep 25 percent spare capacity partly to make zero-downtime rollouts possible. New pods must pass their readiness probe before receiving traffic. The readiness probe polls the ready endpoint every 5 seconds and marks the pod unready after 3 consecutive failures. Readiness should check the things the pod needs to serve, i.e. its database connection and required caches, and nothing else; a readiness probe that checks a downstream service turns that downstream outage into a platform-wide rollout freeze. Liveness probes are deliberately dumber, a process-level check only, because a liveness probe that inspects dependencies restarts healthy pods during downstream incidents. Startup order is not guaranteed, so services must tolerate their dependencies being briefly absent at boot. Configuration changes ship exactly like code: a manifest change in the environment repo, rolled out pod by pod. Secrets rotate through the same mechanism, mounted as files and re-read on change where the service supports it. If a deploy goes wrong, roll back first and investigate second. Rollback is kubectl rollout undo, and the platform target is a rollback completing within 15 minutes of the decision to revert. In practice the undo itself takes about 2 minutes; the 15 minute budget is mostly for noticing and deciding. The deploy that cannot be rolled back is the dangerous one: schema changes, queue format changes, anything a new version writes that an old version cannot read. Those need the expand-and-contract pattern described in the migration guide, and the deploy pipeline will not gate that for you. Deploy freezes: no production deploys on Fridays after 14:00 local time, and none during the December change freeze published by the platform team. The freeze is not about Fridays being unlucky; it is about weekend response capacity being a fraction of weekday capacity. Emergency exceptions to a freeze need sign-off from the on-call lead, and the bar is a live incident, not a missed sprint goal. Observability during rollout: the pipeline watches error rate and p95 latency for the new replica set and pauses the rollout if either degrades against the previous version. A paused rollout pages the deploying engineer, not the platform team; the deployer owns the decision to proceed or undo. Postmortems for failed deploys focus on the gap in the gate, because a human catching a bad deploy means the automation missed it. The platform promise is simple: any engineer can deploy any service safely without knowing kubernetes internals. Every exception to this guide erodes that promise, so exceptions get reviewed monthly and either become features of the pipeline or get closed.

title: Architecture: the logging pipeline
text: Architecture: the logging pipeline. Every container on the platform writes structured JSON logs to stdout, and this document follows a log line from that stdout to a search result. Collection: fluent-bit runs as a daemonset, tails container output, and ships log lines to the Kafka topic logs.raw, which has 12 partitions keyed by service name. Keying by service keeps each service's lines ordered, which matters for multi-line stack traces and for tail-based debugging. Fluent-bit adds cluster, node, and pod metadata at the edge, because enrichment after the fact requires a join someone has to maintain. Kafka is the pipeline's buffer and its backbone. Retention on logs.raw is 72 hours, which is the window the pipeline has to be broken before logs are lost for good. That window is a real budget: the indexer once fell 9 hours behind during a reindex and nothing was lost, but a three-day outage of the indexing tier would eat data. Consumers read logs.raw independently: the indexer, the metrics deriver, and the archive writer each keep their own consumer group and their own offsets. The archive writer copies every line to S3 in hourly Parquet files, so the long-term record survives even when the search cluster does not. The indexer is the consumer people notice. It batches lines and flushes a batch at 5000 documents or after 2 seconds, whichever comes first, trading a bounded delay for fewer, larger writes to the search cluster. Under normal load flushes are size-triggered; the 2 second timer exists for quiet services so their logs still show up promptly. Index mappings are strict: unknown fields are dropped and counted, not indexed, after an incident where one service's free-form field names created forty thousand index fields and stalled the cluster. Log levels are a cost control, not a style choice. Production containers log at info and above; debug logging in production is sampled at 1 percent per service, enough to see the shape of a problem without paying for its full volume. The sampling decision is made at the edge by fluent-bit, so unsampled debug lines never even reach Kafka. Retention in the search cluster is 14 days for info and 30 days for warnings and errors; anything older lives only in the Parquet archive and is queried through the batch engine. Cost note: the search cluster is roughly 70 percent of the pipeline's spend, which is why retention there is short and the archive is the source of truth. Failure modes, in rough order of frequency: a service logging non-JSON, which routes to a quarantine index; a burst filling a partition faster than the indexer drains it, visible as consumer lag; and mapping conflicts from a field changing type. Consumer lag above 5 minutes on the indexer pages the pipeline on-call. Non-JSON bursts do not page anyone; the quarantine index has a dashboard and a weekly review instead. What this pipeline does not do: tracing, metrics aggregation, and alerting all live elsewhere; logs here are for humans reading about the past, and the design accepts seconds of delay to make that reading cheap and complete.

title: Onboarding: the payments service
text: Onboarding: the payments service. Welcome; this is the service where bugs cost actual money, and the guide is organized around the invariants that keep that from happening. Read it before your first change and again after your first month; the second read is the one where it makes sense. The core model is a double-entry ledger. Every movement of money is a transaction with entries that sum to zero across accounts, written once and never edited. The ledger is append-only: corrections are posted as reversal entries, never as updates to existing rows. If you find yourself writing an UPDATE against a ledger table, stop; the schema will fight you and the auditors will fight you harder. Balances are materialized views over entries, recomputed incrementally, and any balance can be re-derived from the entry history alone. That re-derivation runs in CI against a fixture ledger on every merge, so a change that breaks derivability cannot land. External money movement goes through provider adapters, one per payment provider, all implementing the same narrow interface. Providers fail in creative ways: timeouts that succeeded, duplicate webhooks, webhooks out of order, and currency rounding that disagrees with ours by one minor unit. The adapter layer translates that creativity into our invariants, and the adapter test suites are where most of the institutional knowledge lives. Retries are safe because writes are idempotent. Every mutating request carries an idempotency key, and keys are stored in a dedicated table with a unique constraint scoped to a 7 day window. A retried request inside the window returns the stored original response, byte for byte, without touching the ledger again. The 7 day window is a compromise: long enough for any sane retry policy, short enough that the key table stays small; a client retrying after a week gets a fresh execution, and that edge is documented in the client SDKs. Reconciliation is the safety net under everything above. The reconciliation job runs daily at 06:00 UTC, compares our ledger against every provider settlement report, and pages the payments on-call on any nonzero delta. There is no threshold under which a delta is ignored; a one-cent discrepancy has the same page as a thousand-dollar one, because small deltas are how systematic bugs introduce themselves politely. Historically about half of reconciliation pages are provider report timing issues that clear by themselves, and the runbook's first step is checking the report's coverage window. Manual operations exist and are guarded. Refunds above 500 dollars require a second approver in the operations tool, and every manual ledger operation is itself a ledger transaction with an operator id attached. Support can trigger refunds; support cannot post arbitrary entries; nobody can post entries that do not balance. Access to the production database is read-only for everyone, including the team that owns it, and mutations happen through the service or not at all. Local development runs against a provider simulator that replays recorded provider behavior, including the pathological cases; if you add a new provider quirk to an adapter, add the recording that proves it. The paranoia has a purpose: money systems earn trust in years and lose it in an afternoon. When in doubt, make the invariant stricter and the operation slower; payments is the one place where boring and slow outrank clever and fast.

title: Runbook: TLS certificate rotation
text: Runbook: TLS certificate rotation. Scope: every certificate the platform terminates or presents, internal and external, and the small set that still needs a human. The goal state is that rotation is invisible: certificates renew themselves, services reload them without restarting, and this runbook is only opened when something breaks. Internal service certificates come from the internal CA through cert-manager. They are issued with a 90 day validity and renewed automatically at 60 days, giving a 30 day buffer for renewal failures to be noticed and fixed. Renewal is triggered by the cert-manager reconciliation loop, and humans are involved only when a renewal fails; there is no scheduled human step in the happy path. Services consume certificates as mounted files and are expected to re-read them on change; the platform sends SIGHUP to the handful of servers that cannot. A renewal failure is not urgent on day one, and that is the design: the alerting is tuned to catch decay long before expiry. The certificate expiry alert fires when any tracked certificate has fewer than 21 days of validity left. At 21 days the renewal has effectively failed for weeks, since cert-manager retries on a backoff measured in hours, and the remaining buffer is still three weeks of working time. The alert routes to the owning team, not to a central security queue; the platform tracks the inventory, but the owner holds the pager. Expiry alerts are actionable by definition and have no snooze; acknowledging one means fixing the renewal, not silencing the reminder. Public-facing certificates for the main domains follow the same automated path against the public ACME CA, with one wrinkle: the DNS challenge records are managed by the pipeline, and a DNS provider outage during renewal is the one external dependency in the loop. The pipeline retries DNS challenges for 48 hours before paging, which has absorbed every provider blip so far. The legacy partner gateway is the exception this runbook exists for. Two partner integrations pin our client certificate, so rotating it silently breaks them, and their change control is human. The pinned client certificates for the legacy partner gateway are rotated manually, with 14 days of advance notice to both partners, on a date they confirm. The notice period is contractual; shipping the rotation early because the calendar looked clear caused an outage before the contract language existed, which is why the confirmation step is not optional. The manual rotation is a four-step ceremony: generate the new keypair in the HSM, send the certificate to the partners with the switchover date, flip the gateway to present the new certificate at the agreed time, and keep the old one loaded for fallback for 7 days. Rollback is the fallback certificate; if a partner pinning update slips, flip back and reschedule, and the only hard rule is that the old key never leaves the HSM during the overlap. Inventory is the part everyone underestimates. Every certificate, automated or manual, is registered in the certificate inventory with an owner, a source, and a renewal mechanism; unregistered certificates are found by the weekly scanner that walks every listening port in the fleet. The scanner has found forgotten certificates on internal admin panels twice; both times the finding was a missing inventory entry, and once it was also a certificate with 9 days left. The uncomfortable truth of certificate operations is that the failure mode is silent until it is total. Nothing degrades as a certificate ages; it works perfectly and then nothing works at all. Rotation automation, buffers, and inventory exist to convert that cliff into a slope someone is paid to notice.

title: Design: the feature flag system
text: Design: the feature flag system. Flags decouple deploy from release: code ships dark, gets enabled for a slice of traffic, and the blast radius of a bad idea is a config change, not a rollback. This document covers evaluation, targeting, lifecycle, and the kill switch path. Evaluation is client-side. Each service embeds the flag SDK, which polls the flag service for a config snapshot every 30 seconds and evaluates rules locally against request context. Local evaluation means flag checks cost nanoseconds and keep working when the flag service is down; the SDK serves the last good snapshot and a stale snapshot beats no answer. The staleness window is bounded by the poll interval, so a normal flag change reaches the whole fleet within about 30 seconds plus propagation skew. Targeting rules are ordered and first-match: explicit user allowlists, then attribute predicates such as plan tier or region, then percentage rollouts, then the default. Percentage rollouts hash the user id with murmur3 into 10000 stable buckets, so a user's assignment never flickers between requests and ramping from 5 to 10 percent only adds users, never reshuffles them. Bucketing is per flag, salted by the flag key, so being in the 5 percent for one experiment says nothing about the next. Flag evaluation is deterministic given the snapshot and the context; the same request replayed against the same snapshot yields the same answer, which is what makes flag-dependent bugs reproducible. Every flag has an owner, a description, and an expiry date, all required at creation, and the linter blocks flag checks in code that reference a flag the service does not declare. Flags are meant to die. A flag past its expiry date with no activity pages nobody, but a flag stale for 90 days pages its owner in the weekly hygiene report, and the report escalates to the team lead after two ignored cycles. The stale-flag pressure is deliberate: every flag is a fork in the code, and a hundred forgotten forks make every incident investigation slower. Cleanup means removing the check from code first, then archiving the flag; archiving first turns every check into the default and has shipped a surprise before. The kill switch path is the part with different physics. Kill switches bypass the polling cache and propagate through a push channel, taking effect fleet-wide within 2 seconds of the toggle. They exist for exactly two cases: disabling a feature that is actively harming production, and shedding optional load during capacity incidents. Kill switches are boring booleans on purpose; no percentages, no targeting, because the moment you need one is the moment you cannot debug a rules engine. The push channel is tested weekly by toggling a synthetic kill switch and measuring propagation; the 2 second claim is a measured p99, not an aspiration. Flag data is config, not code, but it reviews like code: changes to production flags above 5 percent traffic require a second approver in the flag UI, and every change is audit-logged with who, what, and the diff. Experiments layer on top: an experiment is a percentage rollout plus an assignment event emitted for analysis, and the analysis pipeline joins assignments to outcomes downstream. The flag system failure mode is not outage but entropy: rules nobody remembers, flags nobody owns, and a config snapshot that has quietly become the real program. The countermeasures are ownership, expiry, and the discipline that a flag is a loan against future cleanup, not a gift.

title: Guide: database schema migrations
text: Guide: database schema migrations. Schema changes are deploys with worse rollback options, and this guide is the difference between a migration and an outage. It covers ordering, the expand-and-contract pattern, large-table changes, and the rules the pipeline enforces. Ordering is the first invariant. Migrations run in the deploy pipeline before the new application code rolls out, so every migration must leave a schema that both the old code and the new code can run against. That compatibility requirement is the whole discipline: the database is shared state between two code versions during every single deploy. Expand and contract is how changes stay compatible. Expand first: add the new column, table, or index alongside the old shape, with the new code writing both and reading the old. Migrate the data, verify, then flip reads to the new shape. Contract last: remove the old shape only after nothing reads it. Destructive changes wait one full release cycle after the last code that reads the old shape is gone, so a rollback of the application never lands on a schema that already dropped what it needs. The pipeline enforces the wait mechanically: a migration marked destructive is refused unless the release that stopped reading the column has been in production for a full cycle. Large tables get their own rules, learned the expensive way. Adding a column with a default value rewrites the entire table on Postgres versions before 11, holding a lock for the duration; on the orders table that rewrite was once measured at 40 minutes of write blocking. The rule that came out of it: new columns are added nullable, and defaults are backfilled in batches of 10000 rows with a pause between batches, keeping each transaction short and replication lag bounded. Index creation uses CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, always, and the migration framework rejects the non-concurrent form on tables above a size threshold. Every migration must complete in under 5 minutes or be split into smaller steps; the limit exists because the deploy pipeline holds the release for the migration, and a long migration turns every deploy behind it into a queue. Batched backfills that need longer run as background jobs outside the deploy path, tracked by a progress table, resumable from the last completed batch. Migrations are forward-only in production. Down migrations exist for development convenience and are never run against production; recovering from a bad migration means writing a new forward migration, because down migrations against production data are untested code running in an emergency. Every migration ships in its own pull request with the query plan for any data change on a production-sized dataset, and the reviewer checklist asks one question above all: what happens if this stops halfway. Migrations are wrapped in transactions where the operation allows it; the ones that cannot be, like concurrent index builds, must be idempotent so a retry after a crash converges instead of failing. Naming and numbering are sequential per service, and two migrations landing the same number is a merge conflict, not a runtime surprise. The closing rule is cultural: schema changes are not a place for cleverness. A boring migration that takes three deploys is cheaper than a clever one that takes one deploy and one incident.

title: Policy: alerting and on-call
text: Policy: alerting and on-call. This policy exists to protect two things that trade against each other: production, which needs humans to notice problems, and the humans, who need to sleep. Every alerting decision in it is downstream of one rule: a page is a demand that a human stop what they are doing, including sleeping, right now. Pages must be actionable. If the responder cannot do something about the alert in the moment, it is not a page; it goes to the team Slack channel or a ticket queue instead, and the weekly review decides whether it should exist at all. Symptom-based beats cause-based: page on user-visible symptoms like error rate and latency, not on causes like a full disk on one replica, because causes without symptoms are tickets and symptoms find causes you did not predict. The SLO burn-rate alerts are the backbone. A service pages when it burns error budget at 14.4 times the sustainable rate over 1 hour, or at 6 times over 6 hours; the fast window catches cliffs and the slow window catches smolders. Both windows must be burning for the page to fire, which suppresses the blip that self-heals before a human could act anyway. The math ties pages to consequences: at that fast-window rate for an hour, a 30 day error budget is 2 percent gone, which is exactly the kind of morning a human should hear about. Paging thresholds are owned by the service team, but loosening one below the policy floor needs a documented SLO change, not a quiet edit; the alert config lives in git and deploys through the same review pipeline as code, so every threshold change has an author, a reviewer, and a timestamp. Acknowledgment: a page unacknowledged for 5 minutes escalates to the secondary, and after 10 more minutes to the team lead. The 5 minute acknowledgment target is about arrival, not resolution; ack means a human is looking, and the escalation chain exists for the phone left in the other room, not as a judgment. On-call rotations are weekly, handed off with a written summary of open threads, and a rotation averaging more than 2 pages per night for a quarter triggers a mandatory reliability review of the service, funded before feature work. That threshold has teeth: two services have had roadmaps rewritten by it, and both teams later called it the best thing that happened to the codebase. Alert hygiene is scheduled, not aspirational. The weekly alert review walks every page from the last 7 days and sorts each into actionable, noisy, or duplicate; anything noisy twice in a row is demoted from paging or deleted, and deletions need no ceremony because the alert config git history is the undo button. Runbook links are required on every page; a page without a runbook is allowed to exist for 14 days, the time to write one, and is demoted after that. The runbook standard is low on purpose: three sentences on what the alert means and the first two things to check beat a wiki page nobody maintains. Silences are temporary by construction, expiring in at most 24 hours, because a permanent silence is a deleted alert wearing a disguise. During incidents, the incident commander may silence anything; outside incidents, silencing a page owned by another team needs that team to sign off. Postmortems review the paging record with one question: did the humans find out at the right time. Alerts that fired late get threshold reviews; alerts that never fired for real user pain get created; and the review treats a page that woke someone for nothing as a bug with a cost, filed and fixed like any other. The success metric is not zero pages; a service that never pages is either perfect or unwatched, and only one of those exists. The metric is that every page was worth it, and that number is reviewed quarterly with the same seriousness as uptime.
